summary: This excerpt from Book 11 (part 125) describes the morning of a graduation day in a small town. Girls curl their hair with leads, rags, and palm-leaf fans, and wear simple white dresses. Rebecca and Emma Jane prepare in their room; Rebecca has made a cheesecloth dress with the help of several townswomen, and Emma Jane is tearful, sensing the end of their close friendship. Rebecca has been offered two teaching positions, and as the first bell rings she stands motionless as the class prepares to walk to the church.
one_line: On graduation morning, Rebecca and Emma Jane prepare their cheesecloth dresses while Rebecca weighs two teaching job offers.
key_facts: Girls of the period rolled their hair on leads or papers to achieve curls, and some substituted rags for leads.
Anxious mothers waved palm-leaf fans over their daughters while the hair was set.
The town clock striking ten was chosen as the moment to release the girls from their curling tortures.
Dotted or plain Swiss muslin was the favorite garb for the occasion.
Rebecca had not seen a clear way to a graduating dress until a month before.
Rebecca and Emma Jane visited the Perkins attic and found white butter-muslin or cheesecloth, which they decided would do.
The blacksmith's daughter chose cheesecloth to follow Rebecca's lead rather than dotted Swiss.
Rebecca's dress was finished in sections: the sash by Hannah, waist and sleeves by Mrs. Cobb, and skirt by aunt Jane.
The cheesecloth cost only three or four pennies a yard.
Emma Jane was in a tearful state, feeling that this was the last day of their close intimacy.
Mr. Morrison offered Rebecca two positions the day before.
One position was playing for singing and calisthenics and supervising piano practice of younger girls in a boarding-school, which included educational advantages Miss Maxwell thought valuable.
The other position was an assistant's place in the Edgewood High School, both modest in salary.
When the first bell rang announcing five minutes until the class walked to the church, Rebecca stood motionless and speechless.
